If there is nothing after death, I will at least avoid distressing those present with my lamentations during the time before my death. And my ignorance will not persist with me—that would be an evil—but will soon perish. Prepared like this, Simmias and Cebes, I approach the argument. You, if you listen to me, will give little thought to Socrates, and much more to the truth. If I seem to say anything true, agree with me; if not, oppose me with every argument, taking care that in my eagerness I do not deceive both myself and you, departing like a bee leaving its stinger behind."

div.head: Section 91
div.p: "Let us begin," he said. "First remind me of what you said, if I do not seem to remember. Simmias, I believe, is in doubt and fears that the soul, although more divine and beautiful than the body, perishes before it, being a kind of harmony. Cebes seemed to grant me this: that the soul is more durable than the body. But he argued that no one knows whether the soul, having worn out many bodies, perishes itself when it leaves its last body; and that death might be exactly this—the destruction of the soul, since the body never stops perishing continuously. Are these the things, Simmias and Cebes, that we must examine?" They both agreed that they were. "Now," he asked, "do you reject all the previous arguments, or only some of them?" They said they rejected some, but not others. "What do you say about the argument in which we said learning is recollection, and that since this is so, our soul must necessarily have existed somewhere before being bound in the body?" "I was wondrously persuaded by it then," said Cebes, "and I still hold to it more firmly than any other." "And I hold the same," said Simmias. "I would be very surprised if I ever thought differently about it." Socrates replied, "But you must think differently about it, my Theban friend, if you maintain your opinion that a harmony is something composite, and that the soul is a harmony composed of the elements tensioned in the body. For you surely will not accept your own statement that a harmony was composed and existed before the things from which it was to be composed existed. Or will you accept that?" "Never, Socrates," he said. "Do you perceive," he said, "that this is exactly what happens to your argument when you say the soul exists before entering human form and body, and yet is composed of things that do not yet exist? A harmony is not what you are likening it to. The lyre, the strings, and the unharmonized sounds come first; the harmony is composed last of all, and perishes first. How will this argument harmonize with the other?" "Not at all," said Simmias.

div.head: Section 92
div.p: "And yet," he said, "if an argument about harmony should harmonize with anything, it should be with this one." "It should," said Simmias. "But this one does not harmonize with your view," he said. "Consider: which argument do you choose? That learning is recollection, or that the soul is a harmony?" "The former, much preferred, Socrates," he said. "The latter came to me without proof, from a certain probability and plausibility, which is why most people find it appealing. I know that arguments making their proofs through probabilities are impostors, and if one is not careful, they deceive greatly in geometry and everything else. But the argument about recollection and learning was delivered through an assumption worthy of acceptance. It was said that our soul existed before entering the body exactly as that reality which bears the name 'what it is.' I have accepted this reality sufficiently and rightly, as I am persuaded. Therefore, it is necessary for me, it seems, to accept neither from myself nor from anyone else the assertion that the soul is a harmony." "Consider this as well, Simmias," he said. "Do you think a harmony, or any other composite thing, should be in a state different from the elements from which it is composed?" "By no means." "Nor can it do or suffer anything other than what they do or suffer?" He agreed. "Therefore, a harmony is not naturally suited to lead the things that compose it, but to follow them." He agreed. "It is far from possible for a harmony to move, sound, or do anything contrary to its parts." "Far from it," he said. "Is not every harmony naturally a harmony according to the way it is harmonized?" "I don't understand," he said. "If it is harmonized more, and more fully—if such a thing is possible—would it not be more of a harmony and a fuller one? And if less, and less fully, less of a harmony and a lesser one?" "Certainly." "Is this true of the soul? Is one soul even in the slightest degree more, and more fully, or less, and less fully, a soul than another?" "Not in the least," he said.

div.head: Section 93
div.p: "Come then, by Zeus," he said. "It is said that one soul possesses intelligence and virtue and is good, while another possesses folly and wickedness and is bad. Are these things said truly?" "Truly indeed." "For those who posit that the soul is a harmony, what will they say these things in the soul—virtue and wickedness—are? Will they say they are another harmony and discord? That the good soul is harmonized, and being a harmony, has another harmony within it, while the bad soul is discordant and has no other harmony within it?" "I cannot say," said Simmias, "but clearly someone adopting that hypothesis would say something like that." "But we have already agreed," he said, "that one soul is not more or less a soul than another. And this is an admission that one harmony is not more or less, nor more fully or less fully, a harmony than another. Is that so?" "Certainly." "And what is neither more nor less a harmony is neither more nor less harmonized. Is that true?" "It is." "Does that which is neither more nor less harmonized have a greater or lesser share of harmony, or an equal share?" "An equal share." "Then since no soul is more or less a soul than any other, it is neither more nor less harmonized." "That is so." "Being in this condition, it could not have a greater share of discord or harmony." "No." "Consequently, could one soul share in wickedness or virtue more than another, if wickedness is discord and virtue is harmony?" "It could not." "Or rather, Simmias, by right reasoning, no soul will have any share of wickedness, if it is a harmony. For a harmony, being entirely a harmony, could never share in discord." "Certainly not." "Nor, surely, could a soul, being entirely a soul, share in wickedness." "How could it, from what has been agreed?" "From this reasoning, then, the souls of all living creatures will be equally good, if indeed souls are naturally equally souls." "It seems so to me, Socrates," he said. "Does it seem to you," he asked, "that this is well argued, and that this would happen to our argument if the hypothesis that the soul is a harmony were correct?" "Not in the least," he said.

div.head: Section 94
div.p: "What about all the things within a human being?" he said. "Do you say anything else rules besides the soul, especially an intelligent one?" "I do not." "Does it rule by yielding to the affections of the body, or by opposing them? I mean, for example, when the body has a fever and is thirsty, the soul draws it opposite, toward not drinking. When it is hungry, toward not eating. And in countless other ways, we see the soul opposing the elements of the body. Do we not?" "Certainly." "Did we not also agree earlier that if it were a harmony, it could never sound contrary to the tensions, relaxations, pluckings, and other affections of the elements composing it, but would always follow them and never lead them?" "We did agree," he said. "How could we not?" "But now it appears to be doing the exact opposite. It leads all the things it is supposedly composed of, opposing them in almost everything throughout life, acting as master in every way. It chastises some harshly with pain (as in gymnastics and medicine), and handles others more gently. It threatens some and advises others, conversing with desires, angers, and fears as though it were distinct from them. Just as Homer portrays in the Odyssey, when Odysseus 'struck his chest and rebuked his heart, saying: Bear up, my heart; you endured even worse than this.' Do you think he composed this while believing the soul was a harmony, capable of being led by the body's affections? Rather, he knew it was able to lead and master them, being something far more divine than a harmony." "By Zeus, Socrates, it seems so to me." "Therefore, my excellent friend, it is by no means right for us to say the soul is a harmony. We would apparently be disagreeing both with the divine poet Homer and with ourselves." "That is so," he said.

div.head: Section 95
div.p: "Well then," said Socrates. "The Theban Harmonia seems to have been sufficiently propitiated. But what about Cadmus, Cebes? How shall we appease him, and with what argument?" "I think you will find a way," said Cebes. "This argument against harmony you made so wonderfully it exceeded all my expectations. When Simmias was stating his difficulty, I wondered greatly if anyone could handle his argument. Yet right from your first attack, it could not withstand you. I would not be surprised if the argument of Cadmus met the same fate." "My good man," said Socrates, "do not speak proudly, lest some ill-will overturn the argument about to be spoken. Let that be a concern for the god, but let us come to close quarters in the Homeric manner and test if you say anything worthwhile. The sum of what you are seeking is this: you require it to be proven that our soul is imperishable and immortal, so that a philosopher, about to die and confident that he will fare better there than if he had lived another life, will not be confident with a foolish and vain confidence. Your point is that demonstrating that the soul is strong, god-like, and existed before we were born into human form does not prove immortality. It only proves the soul is long-lasting and existed somewhere an unimaginably long time before, knowing and doing many things. But it was no more immortal for all that. In fact, its very entrance into a human body was the beginning of its destruction, like a disease. It lives this life in distress and finally perishes in what is called death. You say it makes no difference whether it enters a body once or many times, as far as the fear each of us has. For anyone but a fool must fear, if he does not know and cannot prove that it is immortal. I believe this is exactly what you are saying, Cebes. I am repeating it carefully so nothing escapes us, and so you can add or subtract anything if you wish." Cebes replied, "I don't need to add or subtract anything right now. That is exactly what I say."

div.head: Section 96
div.p: Socrates paused for a long time, examining something within himself. Finally, he said, "You seek no small thing, Cebes. For this requires a thorough investigation into the whole cause of coming-to-be and perishing. I will tell you my own experiences concerning these matters, if you wish. Then, if anything I say seems useful to you, you can use it for persuasion regarding what you say." "I certainly wish to hear it," said Cebes. "Listen then, and I will tell you. When I was young, Cebes, I was wonderfully eager for the kind of wisdom they call investigating nature. It seemed an outstanding thing to me to know the causes of everything—why each thing comes to be, why it perishes, and why it exists. I frequently tossed myself up and down, examining first questions like these: Is it when heat and cold undergo a certain putrefaction, as some say, that animals are formed? Is it blood with which we think, or air, or fire? Or none of these, but rather the brain that provides the senses of hearing, sight, and smell, from which memory and opinion arise, and from memory and opinion, once they reach a state of rest, comes knowledge? Investigating further into their perishing, and into the things of the heavens and earth, I ended up thinking I was so completely unsuited for this investigation that nothing could be more so. Let me give you an adequate proof. Things I previously knew clearly—at least as it seemed to me and everyone else—I was so blinded by this investigation that I unlearned even what I thought I knew before! For instance, why a human being grows. I used to think it was clear to everyone that it was because of eating and drinking. When, through food, flesh added itself to flesh, bone to bone, and everything else found its proper addition, then the small mass became large, and the small man became large. That is what I used to think. Does it seem reasonable to you?" "It does," said Cebes. "Consider this further. I used to think my opinion was sufficient when a large man stood next to a small one, that he was taller precisely by a head. And a horse next to a horse. And even more clearly: ten seemed more than eight because two had been added, and the two-cubit length seemed greater than the one-cubit length because it exceeded it by half." "And what is your opinion of them now?" asked Cebes. "By Zeus," he said, "I am far from thinking I know the cause of any of these things. I do not even dare to accept that when one is added to one, either the one to which the addition was made became two, or the added one and the one it was added to became two because of the addition. I marvel that when each of them was separate, each was one and they were not two, but when they came near each other, this became the cause of their becoming two: the meeting of being placed close to each other! Nor can I persuade myself that if someone splits one thing in half, this splitting becomes the cause of its becoming two. That would be the exact opposite cause from before. Before, it was bringing them close together; now, it is moving them apart! Nor can I even persuade myself that I know why 'one' comes to be, or why anything else comes to be, perishes, or exists, following this method of inquiry. So I mix up a different method of my own, and I do not admit this one at all."

div.head: Section 97
div.p: "But hearing someone reading from a book by Anaxagoras—as he said—saying that Mind is what orders and is the cause of all things, I rejoiced in this cause. I thought it was somehow correct that Mind is the cause of all. If this is so, I thought, then the ordering Mind orders everything and places each thing in the way that is best. Therefore, if anyone wishes to find the cause of how each thing comes to be, perishes, or exists, he must find out how it is best for that thing to exist, act, or be acted upon. According to this reasoning, a human being need examine nothing else, concerning himself or others, but what is best and most excellent. And he would automatically know the worse as well, since the knowledge of both is the same. Reasoning this way, I was delighted to think I had found a teacher in the cause of reality according to my own mind: Anaxagoras. I expected he would first tell me whether the earth is flat or round, and having told me, he would add the cause and the necessity, explaining what is best, and why it is better for it to be that way. And if he said it was in the center, he would explain why it is better for it to be in the center. If he could demonstrate this to me, I was prepared to stop longing for any other kind of cause. I was also prepared to learn the same about the sun, the moon, and the other stars, regarding their relative speeds, their turnings, and all their other experiences—how it is best for each of them to act and be acted upon. I never supposed that, having said they were ordered by Mind, he would introduce any other cause for them than that it is best for them to be as they are. I assumed that by giving the cause for each thing and for everything in common, he would explain what is best for each, and the common good for all. I would not have sold my hopes for a great sum of money. I seized the books with great eagerness and read them as quickly as I could, so that I might know the best and the worse as soon as possible."

div.head: Section 98
div.p: "But from this wondrous hope, my comrade, I was suddenly dashed away. For as I proceeded and read further, I saw a man making no use of Mind whatsoever, nor assigning any real causes for the ordering of reality, but giving causes like air, aether, water, and many other absurdities! It seemed to me exactly as if someone said, 'Socrates does everything he does by Mind,' and then, trying to state the causes of each thing I do, he said that the reason I am sitting here now is because my body is composed of bones and sinews; the bones are solid and have joints separating them, while the sinews can be contracted and relaxed, covering the bones along with the flesh and skin holding them together. So, as the bones pivot in their sockets, the relaxation and contraction of the sinews make me able to bend my limbs right now, and that is the cause of my sitting here bent like this! Or again, assigning similar causes for my conversing with you: assigning sounds, air currents, hearings, and countless other such things, neglecting to mention the true causes! Namely, that since the Athenians thought it best to condemn me, I in turn thought it best to sit here, and more just to remain and submit to whatever penalty they command. For, by the dog, I suspect these sinews and bones would have been in Megara or Boeotia long ago, carried there by their opinion of what is 'best,' if I had not thought it more just and noble to endure whatever penalty the city orders, rather than fleeing and running away. To call such things causes is extremely absurd. If someone said that without having bones, sinews, and such things, I could not do what I think is right, he would be speaking the truth. But to say that I do what I do because of them, and not from the choice of what is best—and that this is how Mind acts—is an exceedingly careless way of speaking. It shows a failure to distinguish between the real cause and that without which the cause could never be a cause."

div.head: Section 99
div.p: "This is precisely what the majority of people seem to do, groping in the dark, calling the prerequisite a 'cause,' giving it a name that does not belong to it. Because of this, one man surrounds the earth with a vortex, claiming this keeps it in place under the heavens; another sets the air as a support underneath it, like a broad kneading trough. But the power that places them exactly where it is best for them to be—this they neither seek, nor do they think it has any divine strength. They believe they will someday find a stronger and more immortal Atlas to hold everything together. They do not think the genuinely Good and Binding truly binds and holds anything together. I would most gladly have become anyone's pupil to learn about such a cause and how it works! But since I was deprived of it, unable to find it myself or learn it from another, would you like me to show you, Cebes, how I busied myself with the second-best voyage in search of the cause?" "I would like that immensely," he said. "It seemed to me after this," he said, "when I had grown weary of investigating realities, that I must be careful not to suffer what happens to people looking at the sun during an eclipse. Some of them destroy their eyes if they do not look at the sun's reflection in water or some similar medium. I thought of this, and feared that I might completely blind my soul by looking at things with my eyes and trying to grasp them with my senses. So it seemed to me I must take refuge in accounts (logoi) and examine the truth of realities in them. Perhaps my image is slightly flawed in one respect: I do not entirely admit that one who examines realities in accounts is looking at them in images any more than one who examines them in deeds. But this was the path I started on. Laying down in each case the account I judge to be strongest, whatever seems to harmonize with it I set down as true—both regarding cause and everything else—and whatever does not, I set down as untrue. I wish to make what I mean clearer, because I think you do not yet understand." "Not entirely, by Zeus," said Cebes.

div.head: Section 100
div.p: "But what I am saying is nothing new," he said. "It is what I have never stopped saying, both in past times and in our recent argument. I am going to try to show you the form of cause I have busied myself with, and I return to those much-discussed things, beginning from them. I hypothesize that there is a Beautiful itself by itself, and a Good, and a Great, and all the rest. If you grant me these and agree they exist, I hope to display the cause from them, and discover that the soul is immortal." "Grant that I give them to you," said Cebes, "and hurry to the conclusion." "Consider the next step," he said, "and see if you agree. It appears to me that if anything else is beautiful besides the Beautiful itself, it is beautiful for no other reason than because it partakes of that Beautiful. And I say the same for everything. Do you agree with this kind of cause?" "I agree," he said. "Then I no longer understand those other sophisticated causes. If someone tells me why a thing is beautiful, saying it has a vibrant color, or a specific shape, or something like that, I bid farewell to all of them—for they all confuse me. I hold simply, plainly, and perhaps foolishly to this: nothing else makes it beautiful except the presence of, or communion with, or somehow the sharing in, that Beautiful itself. I do not insist on how it happens, but only that all beautiful things are beautiful by the Beautiful. This seems to me the safest answer to give myself and others. Clinging to this, I think I shall never fall: it is safe to answer that beautiful things are beautiful by the Beautiful. Doesn't it seem so to you?" "It does." "And large things are large by Largeness, and larger things are larger by Largeness, and smaller things are smaller by Smallness?" "Yes." "So you would not accept it if someone said that one man is larger than another by a head, and the smaller is smaller by the very same thing (a head). You would insist you simply mean that everything larger than another is larger by nothing else than Largeness, and the smaller is smaller by nothing else than Smallness. I think you would be afraid of encountering a contrary argument if you said someone is larger by a head: first, that the larger is larger and the smaller is smaller by the exact same thing (a head); and second, that the larger man is larger by a head, which is a small thing—and it is surely monstrous that someone should be large by something small. Would you not fear this?" Cebes laughed and said, "I certainly would."

div.head: Section 101
div.p: "Would you not be afraid to say that ten is more than eight by two, and that this is the cause of its excess, rather than saying it is more by Multitude and because of Multitude? Or that the two-cubit measure is greater than the one-cubit by half, rather than by Largeness? For the fear is the same." "Absolutely," he said. "And further, if one is added to one, would you not beware of saying the addition is the cause of their becoming two, or the splitting if one is divided? Would you not shout loudly that you know no other way each thing comes to be except by partaking of the specific essence of each thing it partakes of? So in these cases, you admit no other cause of becoming two than partaking in Duality. Whatever is to be two must partake in it, and whatever is to be one must partake in Oneness. You would bid farewell to these splittings, additions, and all other such subtleties, leaving them for those wiser than you to answer. Afraid, as the saying goes, of your own shadow and inexperience, you would cling to the safety of the hypothesis and answer accordingly. But if anyone attacked the hypothesis itself, you would let him be and not answer until you had examined whether its consequences agreed or disagreed with one another. And when you had to give an account of the hypothesis itself, you would give it in the same way, hypothesizing another higher hypothesis, whichever seemed best, until you reached something sufficient. You would not mix things up like the contentious debaters, discussing the starting principle and its consequences at the same time, if you wished to discover any of the realities. For those people perhaps care not a whit about this. Their wisdom allows them to mix everything together and still be pleased with themselves. But if you are a philosopher, I think you will do as I say." "You speak perfectly truly," said Simmias and Cebes together.
ECHECRATES. By Zeus, Phaedo, justly so! He seems to me to have explained this with wondrous clarity, even to someone of small intelligence.
PHAEDO. That is exactly what everyone present thought, Echecrates.
ECHECRATES. Even we who were absent and are hearing it now think so. What was said next?

div.head: Section 102
div.p: PHAEDO. I think after these things were granted to him, and it was agreed that each of the Forms exists, and the other things partaking of them take their names from them, he next asked: "If you speak this way, then when you say Simmias is larger than Socrates but smaller than Phaedo, you say both things are in Simmias: Largeness and Smallness?" "I do." "But you agree that the statement 'Simmias surpasses Socrates' is not literally true exactly as spoken? For Simmias does not surpass Socrates because he is Simmias, but because of the largeness he happens to possess. Nor does he surpass Socrates because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has smallness relative to Simmias's largeness." "True." "And he is surpassed by Phaedo, not because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo possesses largeness relative to Simmias's smallness." "That is so." "Thus Simmias is called both small and large, being between the two. Yielding his smallness to the largeness of the one to be surpassed, and presenting his largeness to surpass the smallness of the other." He smiled and said, "It seems I am going to speak like a legal document, but it stands as I say." Simmias agreed. "I say this because I want you to share my opinion. It seems to me that Largeness itself never wills to be simultaneously large and small. And not only that, but the largeness within us never admits the small or wills to be surpassed. One of two things happens: either it flees and retreats when its opposite, the small, approaches, or it perishes when the small arrives. It is not willing to endure and receive smallness, and thereby become something different than what it was. I can receive and endure smallness and still remain exactly who I am, this short man here. But Largeness, being large, never dares to be small. Likewise, the small within us never wills to become or be large, nor does any other opposite, while remaining what it was, will to become and be its opposite. It either goes away or perishes in this affection."

div.head: Section 103
div.p: "It appears so to me entirely," said Cebes. Then someone among those present (I do not clearly remember who it was) said: "By the gods, wasn't the exact opposite of this agreed upon in our earlier arguments? That the larger comes from the smaller, and the smaller from the larger, and that this is exactly how opposites come to be—from opposites? Now it seems to be saying this could never happen." Socrates turned his head, listened, and said, "You recalled that nobly. But you did not perceive the difference between what was said then and what is said now. Then, we were saying that an opposing thing comes to be from an opposing thing. Now, we are saying that the opposite itself could never become opposite to itself—neither the one in us nor the one in nature. Then we spoke of things that possess opposites, calling them by the names of those opposites; but now we speak of the opposites themselves, whose presence gives the things their names. We say those opposites themselves would never consent to come from one another." He looked at Cebes and asked, "Did anything that man said disturb you too, Cebes?" "No," said Cebes, "not this time. Though I admit that many things do trouble me." "Then we agree unconditionally on this: an opposite will never be opposite to itself." "Completely," he said. "Examine this as well, and see if you agree. Is there something you call hot and cold?" "There is." "Are they the same as snow and fire?" "No, certainly not." "Hot is something different from fire, and cold is different from snow." "Yes." "But you think this much: snow, being snow, will never admit the hot, as we said before, and still remain what it was—both snow and hot. But as the hot approaches, it will either retreat before it or perish." "Certainly." "And fire, as the cold approaches, will either retreat or perish; it will never endure receiving the cold and still remain fire and cold." "True," he said. "So the situation with some of these things is this: not only does the Form itself merit its own name for all time, but there is also something else, which is not the Form, but which always possesses its shape whenever it exists. It will be clearer to you from this example. The Odd must always possess this name by which we call it, must it not?" "Certainly." "Is it the only existing thing, or is there something else, which is not the Odd, but which must always be called by the name of the Odd, as well as its own name, because its nature is such that it never abandons the Odd? I mean, for instance, the number three and many others. Consider the number three. Do you not think it must always be called both by its own name and by the name of the Odd, even though the Odd is not the same as three? Such is the nature of three, five, and half of all numbers, that each of them is always odd, though it is not the Odd itself. And two, four, and the other series are always even, though not the Even itself. Do you agree?" "How could I not?" he said.

div.head: Section 104
div.p: "Look closely at what I want to show. It is this: apparently not only do opposites not admit each other, but also things that are not opposite to each other, yet always contain opposites within them—these things do not seem to admit the opposite of what is contained in them. When it approaches, they either perish or retreat. Will we not say that three will sooner perish and suffer anything whatsoever than endure becoming even, while still remaining three?" "We certainly will," said Cebes. "Yet two is not the opposite of three." "No." "Therefore, not only do opposite Forms not endure each other's approach, but certain other things do not endure the approach of opposites." "You speak very truly," he said. "Do you want us to define what sort of things these are, if we can?" he asked. "Certainly." "Would it be these things, Cebes: whatever forces the thing it occupies not only to have its own idea, but also the idea of some opposite?" "How do you mean?" "As we said just now. You surely know that whatever the idea of three occupies must necessarily be not only three, but also odd." "Certainly." "And I say that the idea opposite to the form that accomplishes this can never come into that thing." "It cannot." "And what accomplished this? Was it not the idea of the Odd?" "Yes." "And opposite to this is the idea of the Even?" "Yes." "Therefore, the idea of the Even will never come to three." "Never." "So three has no share in the Even." "It has no share." "So three is uneven." "Yes." "This is what I meant when defining the kind of things that, though not opposite to a certain thing, do not admit that opposite. Just as the three, not being opposite to the Even, nonetheless does not admit it, because it always brings the opposite along with it. And two brings the opposite to the Odd, and fire brings the opposite to the Cold, and so on. See if you would define it this way: not only does an opposite not admit an opposite, but also, whatever brings an opposite into whatever it approaches will never admit the oppositeness to the thing brought. Recollect it again, for there is no harm in hearing it often. Five will not admit the idea of the Even, nor will ten, its double, admit the idea of the Odd. The double is opposite to something else, yet it will not admit the idea of the Odd. Nor will one-and-a-half or other such fractions admit the idea of the Whole, nor will a third, and so on. If you follow and agree." "I agree most vehemently and I follow," he said.

div.head: Section 105
div.p: "Tell me again from the beginning," he said. "And do not answer exactly what I ask, but imitate me. I see a different safe answer beyond the first one I mentioned, derived from what has just been said. If you were to ask me, 'What must come into a body for it to be hot?' I will not give you the safe, ignorant answer, 'Heat,' but a more sophisticated one from our current discussion: 'Fire.' And if you ask, 'What must come into a body to make it sick?' I will not say 'Disease,' but 'Fever.' If you ask what makes a number odd, I will not say 'Oddness,' but 'Oneness.' Do you understand sufficiently what I mean?" "Sufficiently," he said. "Answer me then," he said, "what must come into a body for it to be living?" "Soul," he said. "Is this always so?" "How could it not be?" he said. "Therefore, soul always brings life to whatever it occupies?" "It does indeed," he said. "Is there an opposite to life, or not?" "There is," he said. "What is it?" "Death." "Then soul will absolutely never admit the opposite of what it always brings with it, as we agreed from our previous arguments?" "Most emphatically," said Cebes. "What then? What did we just call the thing that does not admit the idea of the Even?" "Uneven," he said. "And the thing that does not admit the Just, or the Musical?" "Unmusical, and Unjust." "Well then. What do we call that which does not admit death?" "Immortal," he said. "Does the soul not admit death?" "No." "Therefore, the soul is immortal." "It is immortal." "Very well," he said. "Can we say this has been proven? What do you think?" "Very adequately, Socrates."

div.head: Section 106
div.p: "What about this, Cebes? If the Uneven were necessarily imperishable, would not three be imperishable?" "How could it not be?" "And if the Un-hot were necessarily imperishable, whenever anyone brought heat to snow, the snow would retreat intact and unmelted? For it could not perish, nor could it stay and admit the heat." "True," he said. "In the same way, I suppose, if the Un-coolable were imperishable, when something cold approached fire, the fire would never go out or perish, but would retreat safe." "Necessarily." "Must we not say the same about the Immortal? If the Immortal is also imperishable, it is impossible for the soul to perish when death approaches it. From what has been said, it will not admit death, nor will it be dead, just as three will not be even, nor will the Odd itself; nor will fire be cold, nor the heat in the fire. 'But what prevents the Odd from perishing when the Even approaches,' someone might say, 'and becoming Even instead?' To him we could not argue that it does not perish, for the Uneven is not imperishable. If we had agreed it was imperishable, we could easily argue that when the Even approaches, the Odd and the three depart and flee. And we could argue the same about fire, heat, and the rest. Right?" "Certainly." "So now, concerning the Immortal: if we agree that it is imperishable, then the soul would be imperishable as well as immortal. If not, we need another argument." "But there is no need of another on that account," he said. "For what else could escape destruction if the Immortal, being everlasting, admits destruction?"

div.head: Section 107
div.p: "I think everyone would agree," said Socrates, "that the god, the Form of Life itself, and whatever else is immortal, never perishes." "Everyone, by Zeus," he said, "all men and even more so, the gods." "Since the immortal is also indestructible, must not the soul, if it is immortal, also be imperishable?" "With great necessity." "Therefore, when death approaches a human being, the mortal part of him dies, it seems, but the immortal part retreats safely, uncorrupted, making way for death." "It appears so." "Then beyond all doubt, Cebes, the soul is immortal and imperishable, and our souls will truly exist in Hades." "For my part, Socrates," said Cebes, "I have nothing to say against this, nor any reason to doubt your arguments. But if Simmias or anyone else has anything to say, it is better they do not stay silent. For I do not know to what other time they could defer the matter if they wish to speak or hear about these things." "Nor do I," said Simmias, "have any further doubts based on what has been said. Yet, considering the magnitude of the subject we are discussing, and mindful of human weakness, I am forced to retain some lingering doubt in myself about what we have said." "Not only that, Simmias," said Socrates, "you speak well; even our first hypotheses, however trustworthy they seem, should be examined more clearly. If you analyze them adequately, I think you will follow the argument as far as it is possible for a human being to follow. And if this itself becomes clear, you will seek no further." "What you say is true," he said. "But it is right to think about this, gentlemen: if the soul is immortal, it demands our care not only for this time we call life, but for all time. The danger now appears terrible if one neglects it. If death were an escape from everything, it would be a godsend for the wicked to die and be rid of their body, and their soul, and their wickedness all at once. But as it is, since the soul appears immortal, there is no other escape or salvation from evils for it except to become as good and wise as possible. For the soul goes to Hades carrying nothing else with it but its education and upbringing, which are said to bring the greatest benefit or harm to the deceased right from the very beginning of the journey there."

div.head: Section 108
div.p: "It is said that when a person dies, the guiding spirit (daimon) assigned to him in life leads him to a certain place where the dead must gather to be judged before traveling to Hades, guided by the one appointed to bring them from here to there. Once they have received what they must and spent the required time, another guide brings them back here over many long cycles of time. The journey is not as Aeschylus's Telephus describes it. He says the path to Hades is simple, but to me it seems neither simple nor single. If it were, there would be no need of guides, for no one could lose the way on a single path. In truth, it has many forks and crossways—I say this based on the sacrifices and customs observed here. The orderly and wise soul follows its guide and is not ignorant of its present state. But the soul that eagerly desires the body, as I said before, flutters about the body and the visible place for a long time. Only after much resistance and suffering is it forcibly dragged away by its appointed spirit. When it arrives where the others are, if it is impure and has committed some wrong—either participating in unjust murders or similar deeds kin to these—all the other souls flee from it and turn away. They refuse to be its fellow traveler or guide, and it wanders alone in complete perplexity until a certain timespan has passed. When that time is over, it is carried by necessity into its fitting habitation. But the soul that has passed through life purely and moderately finds gods as fellow travelers and guides, and each dwells in the place fitting for it. There are many wondrous places on the earth, and the earth itself is neither of the nature nor the size supposed by those who usually discourse about it. This I have been persuaded of by a certain person." Simmias said, "What do you mean, Socrates? I have heard many things about the earth myself, but not these things you are persuaded of. I would gladly hear them." "Well, Simmias, I do not think it requires the art of Glaucus to narrate what these things are. But to prove they are true seems too hard for the art of Glaucus. I might not be able to do it, and even if I knew how, the time remaining in my life does not seem sufficient for such a long account. Nevertheless, nothing prevents me from describing the shape of the earth as I am persuaded it is, and its regions." "That is sufficient," said Simmias.

div.head: Section 109
div.p: "First," he said, "I am persuaded that if the earth is spherical and in the middle of the heavens, it needs neither air nor any other such necessity to keep from falling. The uniformity of the heavens themselves in every direction, and the equilibrium of the earth itself, are sufficient to hold it. A thing in equilibrium situated in the middle of a uniform medium will have no reason to incline more or less in any direction; being uniform, it will remain without inclining. This is the first thing I am persuaded of." "And rightly so," said Simmias. "Further," he said, "I believe it is very large, and that we who live between the Pillars of Heracles and the Phasis river dwell in only a small part of it, living around the sea like ants or frogs around a pond. Many other people live in many other such regions. For there are many hollows all over the earth, of various shapes and sizes, into which water, mist, and air have flowed together. But the earth itself is pure and lies in the pure heavens, where the stars are, which those who discuss such things call the aether. What flows together into the hollows of the earth is merely the sediment of the aether. We are unaware that we are living in the hollows of the earth and think we live on its upper surface. It is as if someone living at the bottom of the sea thought he was living on the surface, and seeing the sun and stars through the water, thought the sea was the sky. Because he is sluggish and weak, he has never reached the top of the sea, nor lifted his head above the water to see how much purer and more beautiful our region is than his, nor has he heard it from anyone who has seen it. This is exactly what has happened to us. We live in a hollow of the earth, yet assume we live on the top of it. We call the air 'heaven', as though it were the heaven through which the stars run. The truth is the same: because of our weakness and sluggishness, we cannot travel to the upper limit of the air. If someone could reach the top, or grow wings and fly up, he would peek over—just as fish popping their heads out of the sea look upon our world—and he would look upon the world there. If his nature could endure the sight, he would know that it is the true heaven, the true light, and the true earth. For this earth of ours, its stones, and the entire region here are corrupted and eaten away, just as things in the sea are by the salt water. Nothing worth mentioning grows in the sea, nor is there anything perfect; there are only caves, sand, immeasurable mud, and mire wherever there is earth—none of it worthy of comparison with our beautiful things. But the things there would appear to far surpass the things we have here. If it is right to tell a story, Simmias, it is worth hearing what the things on the true earth beneath the heavens are really like." "Indeed, Socrates," said Simmias, "we would gladly hear this story."

div.head: Section 110
div.p: "Well then, my comrade, it is said first of all that this true earth, if viewed from above, looks like one of those twelve-piece leather balls, variegated, distinguished by colors. The colors used by our painters here are like faint samples of them. There, the entire earth is made of such colors, but much brighter and purer than ours. Part of it is purple of wondrous beauty, part golden, and part entirely white—whiter than chalk or snow. And it is composed of all the other colors as well, more numerous and beautiful than any we have ever seen. Even the hollows of the earth, filled with water and air, present a certain color that gleams amid the variety of the other colors, so that the whole appears as one continuous, multicolored vision. Growing on this earth are trees, flowers, and fruits in proportion to its beauty. The mountains and stones are smoother, more transparent, and of more beautiful colors. Our precious stones here—sardian, jasper, emeralds, and all such—are merely fragments of those stones. There, every single stone is like that, and even more beautiful. The reason is that those stones are pure; they are not eaten away or corrupted, as ours are, by the rot and brine of the sediment gathered here, which brings ugliness and disease to stones, earth, animals, and plants. The true earth is adorned with all these stones, as well as with gold, silver, and other such things. They are exposed on the surface, numerous, massive, and scattered everywhere, so that seeing the earth is a sight for blessed spectators. There are many living creatures on it, including human beings. Some dwell inland, some dwell along the shores of the air—just as we live by the sea—and some live on islands surrounded by air, situated near the mainland. In a word, what water and sea are for our needs, air is for them; and what air is to us, aether is to them. Their seasons are so well-tempered that they are free from disease and live much longer than we do. In sight, hearing, intelligence, and all such faculties, they surpass us by the same margin that air is purer than water, and aether purer than air. They have sacred groves and temples of the gods, in which the gods truly dwell. They hear the voices and prophecies of the gods, and have direct contact and communion with them. They see the sun, moon, and stars exactly as they are, and their happiness in all other respects follows this."

div.head: Section 111
div.p: "Such is the nature of the whole earth and the things around it. In the earth itself, around its hollows, there are many regions. Some are deeper and more open than the one we dwell in; others are deeper with a narrower opening; and still others are shallower than ours and broader. All these are connected underground in many places by passages, some narrower, some wider, so that large quantities of water flow from one to another, as if into mixing bowls. And there are huge, unceasing underground rivers of hot and cold waters, and fire, and great rivers of liquid mud, some clearer, some thicker, like the rivers of mud that flow in Sicily before the lava, and the lava itself. These regions are filled by whichever river happens to flow into them at the time. A kind of oscillation within the earth moves all these up and down. The nature of this oscillation is something like this: One of the chasms in the earth happens to be especially large and goes straight through the entire earth. This is the one Homer spoke of: 'Far away, where the deepest abyss lies beneath the earth.' This he and many other poets have called Tartarus. Into this chasm all rivers flow together, and from it they flow out again. Each river takes on the nature of the earth through which it flows. The reason they all flow out and into here is that this liquid has no bottom or resting place. So it oscillates and surges up and down, and the air and wind around it do the same. They follow it when it rushes to the far side of the earth, and when it rushes back here. Just as the breath flows in and out during respiration, so the wind oscillating with the liquid causes terrible and unimaginable blasts coming in and out. When the water retreats into the region we call 'below,' it flows into the rivers of that region and fills them like an irrigation ditch. When it leaves there and rushes 'here,' it fills our rivers again. Once filled, they flow through channels and through the earth, arriving at those places to which each makes its way, creating seas, lakes, rivers, and springs. From there they sink back into the earth, some taking longer, winding paths, some shorter, and empty back into Tartarus—some much lower than where they were pumped out, others only slightly. But all pour in below their point of outflow. Some flow in on the opposite side from where they came out, others on the same side. There are even those that make a complete circle, coiling once or even several times around the earth like serpents, before descending as low as possible to pour back in. It is possible to descend as far as the center from either side, but no further, for the opposite side is an uphill climb for streams from either direction."

div.head: Section 112
div.p: "There are many large and diverse rivers, but among this multitude four stand out. The largest of these, flowing the outermost circle, is the one called Oceanus. Opposite to it, flowing in the contrary direction, is Acheron. It flows through desert places and, sinking beneath the earth, arrives at the Acherusian Lake. This is where the souls of most of the dead arrive, and after staying their destined time—some longer, some shorter—they are sent back to be born as living creatures. Between these two a third river issues forth. Near its source, it pours into a huge region burning with much fire and creates a lake larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From there it moves in a circle, muddy and murky, coiling around within the earth until it reaches the edge of the Acherusian Lake, though mingling with its waters. After coiling multiple times underground, it pours into a lower part of Tartarus. This river is called Pyriphlegethon, and its fiery streams throw off fragments wherever they reach the surface of the earth. Opposite this, the fourth river falls first into a terrible, wild region which is entirely of an indigo hue, called the Stygian region, and the lake it forms is called the Styx. Plunging into this lake and acquiring terrible powers in its water, the river dips beneath the earth, spiraling opposite to Pyriphlegethon and meeting it at the Acherusian Lake from the contrary side. Its water never mixes with any other, but after circling around, it pours into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. The name of this river, the poets say, is Cocytus."

div.head: Section 113
div.p: "Since this is how nature arranged these things, when the dead arrive at the place where the guiding spirit leads each one, first they are judged—both those who have lived noble, holy lives and those who have not. Those whose lives are judged to have been moderate proceed to Acheron, embark on the vessels prepared for them, and arrive at the lake. There they dwell, undergoing purification. By paying the penalty for their wrongdoings, they are absolved of any injustice they committed, and receive rewards for their good deeds, each according to his merit. But those judged incurable because of the magnitude of their sins—having committed many great sacrileges, many unjust and illegal murders, or such things—these the fitting destiny hurls into Tartarus, from which they never emerge. Those judged to have committed curable but great sins—for example, doing violence to a father or mother out of anger, but repenting for the rest of their lives, or committing murder in a similar way—must also fall into Tartarus. However, after they have fallen in and stayed there for a year, the surge casts them out: the murderers along Cocytus, and the strikers of parents along Pyriphlegethon. When they are carried along and arrive at the Acherusian Lake, they cry out and call to those they murdered or outraged. They beg and entreat them to allow them to enter the lake and receive them. If they persuade them, they enter and their troubles cease. If not, they are swept back into Tartarus, and from there back into the rivers, and they do not stop suffering until they have persuaded those they wronged. For this was the penalty imposed on them by the judges. But those judged to have lived exceptionally holy lives are the ones freed and released from these regions in the earth, as if from prisons. They ascend to the pure dwelling place above and live upon the earth. And among these, those who have sufficiently purified themselves by philosophy live entirely without bodies for the rest of time, arriving at dwelling places even more beautiful than these, which are not easy to describe, nor is there sufficient time now."

div.head: Section 114
div.p: "But for the sake of these very things we have described, Simmias, one must do everything to partake of virtue and wisdom in life. For the prize is noble, and the hope is great. To confidently assert that these things are exactly as I have described is not fitting for a sensible man. But that this, or something like it, is true concerning our souls and their dwelling places—since the soul is clearly immortal—seems to me fitting and worth taking a risk on for someone who believes it. For the risk is a noble one, and one must sing such charms to oneself. That is why I have prolonged this story for so long. Because of these things, a man should have confidence regarding his own soul if, during his life, he bade farewell to the pleasures and adornments of the body—considering them alien and thinking they do more harm than good—and earnestly pursued the pleasures of learning. By adorning his soul not with alien ornaments, but with its own—moderation, justice, courage, freedom, and truth—he awaits his journey to Hades, ready to go whenever destiny calls. You, Simmias, Cebes, and the rest of you, will each make this journey at your appointed time in the future. But for me, as a tragic character might say, destiny calls right now. It is just about time for me to go to the bath. For it seems better to drink the poison after bathing, and save the women the trouble of washing a corpse."

div.head: Section 115
div.p: When he said this, Crito asked, "Very well, Socrates. What instructions do you leave for these men or for me about your children or anything else? What could we do that would be most pleasing to you?" "What I am always saying, Crito," he said. "Nothing new. If you take care of yourselves, whatever you do will be pleasing to me, to mine, and to yourselves, even if you do not promise it now. But if you neglect yourselves and refuse to walk in the footsteps of what has been said today and in the past, no matter how many solemn promises you make now, you will accomplish nothing." "We will eagerly strive to do as you say," said Crito. "But how shall we bury you?" "However you wish," he said, "provided you can catch me and I do not escape you." He laughed softly, looked at us, and said, "I cannot persuade Crito, gentlemen, that I am this Socrates here who is conversing and ordering each part of the argument. He thinks I am the one he will soon see as a corpse, and asks how to bury me! As for the long argument I just made—that when I drink the poison, I will no longer remain with you, but will depart to the joys of the blessed—I seem to be saying this in vain to comfort both you and myself. Please stand as guarantors for me to Crito, in the opposite way he stood guarantor for me before the judges. He guaranteed I would stay. You must guarantee that I will not stay after I die, but will depart. Thus Crito will bear it more easily, and when he sees my body being burned or buried, he will not grieve for me as though I were suffering terrible things. Nor will he say at the funeral that he is laying out Socrates, or carrying out Socrates, or burying Socrates. For know well, excellent Crito, that to speak improperly is not only an error in itself, but it plants a kind of evil in the soul. You must be confident, and say that you are burying my body. Bury it however pleases you and however you think is most customary."

div.head: Section 116
div.p: After saying this, he stood up and went into a room to bathe, and Crito followed him, telling us to wait. We waited, discussing the argument among ourselves and reflecting on it, and then talking about the greatness of the misfortune that had befallen us, truly feeling that we were losing a father and would live the rest of our lives as orphans. When he had bathed, his children were brought to him—he had two little sons and one older—and the women of his household came. He spoke with them in Crito's presence, gave his final instructions, and then told the women and children to leave, and returned to us. It was already near sunset, for he had spent a long time inside. He came and sat down, fresh from the bath, and did not say much after that. The officer of the Eleven came and stood before him. "Socrates," he said, "I will not blame you as I blame others, who get angry and curse me when I order them to drink the poison under the magistrates' compulsion. During this time I have found you the noblest, gentlest, and best man who has ever come here. I know well that you are not angry with me now, but with them, for you know who is responsible. You know what I have come to say. Farewell, and try to bear what is necessary as easily as possible." He burst into tears, turned around, and went out. Socrates looked up at him and said, "Farewell to you too. We will do as you say." To us he added, "How courteous the man is! All the time I have been here he would come to see me and talk with me occasionally, the best of men. And now how genuinely he weeps for me! Come, Crito, let us obey him. Let someone bring the poison, if it is ground. If not, let the man grind it." Crito said, "But Socrates, I think the sun is still on the mountains and has not yet set. Besides, I know others have taken it very late, long after the order was given, dining and drinking well, and even enjoying the company of those they desired. Do not hurry; there is still time." Socrates replied, "It is reasonable for those men to do as you say, Crito, for they think they gain something by doing it. And it is equally reasonable for me not to do it. I think I gain nothing by drinking it a little later, except becoming ridiculous in my own eyes by clinging to life and sparing it when nothing is left. Go on," he said, "obey me and do not refuse."

div.head: Section 117
div.p: Hearing this, Crito nodded to the slave standing nearby. The slave went out, was gone for some time, and returned bringing the man who was to administer the poison, carrying it ground in a cup. Seeing the man, Socrates said, "Well, my good man, you know about these things; what must I do?" "Nothing else," he said, "but drink it and walk around until your legs feel heavy. Then lie down, and it will act on its own." At the same time he handed the cup to Socrates. Socrates took it very cheerfully, Echecrates, without a tremor, without changing color or his expression. Looking at the man keenly under his brows, as he usually did, he asked, "What do you say about pouring a libation to a deity from this drink? Is it permitted or not?" "We grind just the amount we think is the right measure to drink, Socrates," he said. "I understand," he said. "But surely it is permitted and necessary to pray to the gods that my journey from here to there may be fortunate. That is my prayer, and may it be so." With these words, he raised the cup and drank it off quite easily and calmly. Until then, most of us had been able to restrain our weeping reasonably well. But when we saw him drinking, and that he had finished drinking, we could hold back no longer. My own tears came flowing in a flood against my will, so I covered my face and wept for myself—certainly not for him, but for my own misfortune in being deprived of such a comrade. Crito had gotten up and moved away even before I did, unable to restrain his tears. Apollodorus, who had not stopped weeping at all previously, now roared aloud, crying and grieving so much that he broke the heart of everyone present, except Socrates himself. "What are you doing, you strange men!" he said. "It was mainly for this reason that I sent the women away, so they would not create such a disturbance. I have heard that one must die in auspicious silence. Be quiet and bear up."

div.head: Section 118
div.p: When we heard this, we were ashamed and checked our tears. He walked around, and when he said his legs were heavy, he lay down on his back, just as the man had instructed. The man who gave him the poison touched him, and after a while examined his feet and legs. He pinched his foot hard and asked if he felt it. Socrates said no. After that, he pressed his shins, and moving upwards like this, showed us that he was growing cold and stiff. Socrates himself touched his body and said that when it reached his heart, he would be gone. Already the cold was reaching his abdomen. He uncovered his face—for he had covered it—and spoke his last words: "Crito," he said, "we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay the debt and do not neglect it." "It shall be done," said Crito. "Is there anything else you want to say?" To this question he made no reply. After a short time, there was a movement. The man uncovered him; his eyes were fixed. Seeing this, Crito closed his mouth and his eyes. Such was the end of our comrade, Echecrates. A man of whom we may say that, of all those of his time whom we experienced, he was the best, the wisest, and the most just.
